newsitem.title: UK: Human rights to dominate UK foreign policy.
newsitem.headline: Human rights to dominate UK foreign policy.

text.p: The new British government intends to push human rights to the forefront of its foreign policy and will take a much closer look at companies that wish to export arms to "sensitive" countries, officials said on Tuesday.

They said Foreign Secretary Robin Cook, appointed last week in the wake of Labour's crushing election win, also intended to put more emphasis on global issues such as the environment and boosting the work done by the United Nations.
"One major new thread in government policy will be the application of human rights," an official told reporters.
"This is at the centre of policy and will have a good deal of relevance in new procedures to be set up on defence exports and so on."

When in opposition Cook attacked the previous Conservative government for turning a blind eye to exports of arms and material to countries such as Iraq and made clear he would introduce new procedures once in power.

"No individual countries have been scrutinised yet but each application (to export defence equipment) will be looked at very closely in the case of sensitive countries," the official said. More details should become clear during a parliamentary debate on foreign affairs next Thursday.
Cook has already promised to slap an immediate ban on British sales of landmines and the publication of an annual report on strategic exports, including defence equipment.

He backs the idea of a Europe-wide code of conduct on arms sales, saying Britain has the right to maintain its competitive edge in the arms market but must also accept responsibility to ensure that market is properly regulated.

Officials said the stress on human rights lay behind Cook's announcement earlier on Tuesday that Britain was willing to host an international conference on what to do about the millions of dollars worth of gold seized by the Nazis in World War Two. Some of it has been held in Swiss bank accounts since the war.
Cook belongs to the left wing of the Labour partty, which has continually taken a more internationalist tone in world affairs.

"He will want to give a lot of emphasis to the global agenda -- the environment, the United Nations and bolstering the economic social and peacekeeping activities of the United Nations," the official said.
Cook planned to hold talks with U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright as soon as possible, the official added.

Labour has already tried to improve relations with the European Union by pledging to scrap the increasingly antagonistic tone taken by the previous government but the officials made clear that some stances would remain unchanged.
Officials said Cook wanted to keep the troubled Middle East peace policy alive and backed NATO's plans for expansion.
The new foreign secretary also reviewed the structure of his ministry and would issue a mission statement on its goals next week.
"He wants to see a better public understanding of the relationship of foreign policy to the domestic agenda of the government in terms of jobs, trade, etc," the official said.
Cook has already invited film director David Puttnam to make a film on the Foreign Office and its aims which would be distributed to British embassies and representations worldwide.
Cook had also made it clear that he wanted to see more top posts occupied by women and people from ethnic minorities.
